Malicious litellm_init.pth startup hook dropped in site-packages (CVE-2026-42208) AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of the credential-stealer `litellm_init.pth` startup hook shipped by the compromised litellm 1.82.7/1.82.8 wheels, which Python auto-executes on interpreter startup with no import. Article-specific because the filename and site-packages location are unique to this supply-chain payload. Rationale: The `litellm_init.pth` filename in `site-packages/` is a unique, high-fidelity artifact of the CVE-2026-42208 payload named directly in the advisory and confirmed by Snyk/NetSPI/BerriAI issue #24512 (34,628-byte .pth). No legitimate package ships a file with this exact name. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/24512 • https://snyk.io/blog/poisoned-security-scanner-backdooring-litellm/ • https://www.netspi.com/blog/executive-blog/ai-ml-pentesting/litellm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-42208
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A local security-audit or IR script writing a decoy litellm_init.pth as a canary/test file
  • Backup or file-integrity tooling restoring an archived site-packages tree containing the artifact
  • Developer intentionally reproducing the IOC in a sandbox for research
  • A remediation script quarantining the file to a new path (rename event)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","pip","uv.exe") or ActionType == "FileCreated"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA256 of the dropped file and the InitiatingProcess (expect pip/python during install); identify which project's requirements pulled litellm 1.82.7/1.82.8. 2) Contain: isolate the host, delete the litellm_init.pth, and force-rotate every credential reachable from that environment (AWS/GCP/Azure keys, SSH keys, kubeconfig, DB creds, CI/CD secrets). 3) Hunt: search all build agents and dev workstations for the same filename, pin litellm>=1.83.7,!=1.82.8, and pivot to the network beacon UC (models.litellm.cloud) to confirm exfil occurred.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "litellm_init.pth"
| where FolderPath has "site-packages"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "litellm_init.pth"
| where TargetFilePath has "site-packages"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Malicious litellm_init.pth Startup Hook Dropped (CVE-2026-42208)
id: 6f3d1c8a-2b4e-4a1f-9c77-1e2f9a0b7d31
description: Detects creation of the litellm_init.pth credential-stealer startup hook from the compromised litellm 1.82.7/1.82.8 wheels
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-98x5-vq43-vc5p
  - https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/24512
  - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-42208
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/07
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1546.016
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '\litellm_init.pth'
    TargetFilename|contains: 'site-packages'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\litellm_init.pth OR *\site-packages\* AND *litellm_init.pth)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/litellm_init\.pth$/i | regex("site-packages", field=TargetFileName) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="litellm_init.pth" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where like(file_path,"%site-packages%") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="litellm_init.pth" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where like(file_path,"%site-packages%") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
litellm supply-chain exfil beacon to models.litellm.cloud (CVE-2026-42208) AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections/DNS to models.litellm.cloud, the exfiltration endpoint the compromised litellm wheel POSTs AES-256/RSA-encrypted stolen credentials to. Article-specific because this domain is the hard-coded C2/exfil sink for CVE-2026-42208, not a generic egress heuristic. Rationale: models.litellm.cloud is the exact hard-coded exfil endpoint cited in the advisory and independently confirmed by Snyk, NetSPI, Miggo and BerriAI issue #24512 as the AES-256/RSA POST sink; any resolution of it is a confirmed second-source IOC, not a heuristic. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/24512 • https://snyk.io/blog/poisoned-security-scanner-backdooring-litellm/ • https://www.miggo.io/post/rce-in-litellm-cve-2026-42208-how-two-vulnerabilities-and-36-hours-turn-an-ai-gateway-into-a-backdoor • https://www.netspi.com/blog/executive-blog/ai-ml-pentesting/litellm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1567 T1041 T1552.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel/EDR product performing sinkhole or reputation lookups against the known-bad domain
  • A SOC analyst manually browsing to the domain during triage
  • A DNS security appliance pre-resolving blocklist entries for enrichment
  • Passive DNS/telemetry-replay tooling replaying historic captures
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the request (expect python.exe/pip) and whether the connection succeeded vs was blocked; correlate the host with the litellm_init.pth file UC. 2) Contain: block models.litellm.cloud and *.litellm.cloud at proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and treat all locally reachable secrets as compromised — rotate immediately. 3) Hunt: sweep DNS/proxy logs org-wide for any prior resolution of the domain to scope every affected build agent and developer host, and audit CI/CD secret stores for anomalous use of the exposed credentials.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "models.litellm.cloud"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "models.litellm.cloud"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses = Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("71e35aef03099cd1f2d6446734273025a163597de93912df321ef118bf135238", "a0d229be8efcb2f9135e2ad55ba275b76ddcfeb55fa4370e0a522a5bdee0120b", "6cf223aea68b0e8031ff68251e30b6017a0513fe152e235c26f248ba1e15c92a") or SHA1 in~ ("71e35aef03099cd1f2d6446734273025a163597de93912df321ef118bf135238", "a0d229be8efcb2f9135e2ad55ba275b76ddcfeb55fa4370e0a522a5bdee0120b", "6cf223aea68b0e8031ff68251e30b6017a0513fe152e235c26f248ba1e15c92a") or MD5 in~ ("71e35aef03099cd1f2d6446734273025a163597de93912df321ef118bf135238", "a0d229be8efcb2f9135e2ad55ba275b76ddcfeb55fa4370e0a522a5bdee0120b", "6cf223aea68b0e8031ff68251e30b6017a0513fe152e235c26f248ba1e15c92a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("71e35aef03099cd1f2d6446734273025a163597de93912df321ef118bf135238", "a0d229be8efcb2f9135e2ad55ba275b76ddcfeb55fa4370e0a522a5bdee0120b", "6cf223aea68b0e8031ff68251e30b6017a0513fe152e235c26f248ba1e15c92a") or SHA1 in~ ("71e35aef03099cd1f2d6446734273025a163597de93912df321ef118bf135238", "a0d229be8efcb2f9135e2ad55ba275b76ddcfeb55fa4370e0a522a5bdee0120b", "6cf223aea68b0e8031ff68251e30b6017a0513fe152e235c26f248ba1e15c92a") or MD5 in~ ("71e35aef03099cd1f2d6446734273025a163597de93912df321ef118bf135238", "a0d229be8efcb2f9135e2ad55ba275b76ddcfeb55fa4370e0a522a5bdee0120b", "6cf223aea68b0e8031ff68251e30b6017a0513fe152e235c26f248ba1e15c92a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["71e35aef03099cd1f2d6446734273025a163597de93912df321ef118bf135238", "a0d229be8efcb2f9135e2ad55ba275b76ddcfeb55fa4370e0a522a5bdee0120b", "6cf223aea68b0e8031ff68251e30b6017a0513fe152e235c26f248ba1e15c92a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)

        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,

    ( ImProcessCreate

        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)

                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Backpropagate training UI publicly exposed via 'backprop ui --share' (CVE-2026-48797) AIDelivery High
Hunts process executions of the Backpropagate CLI launching the Reflex training UI with the --share (public exposure) or --auth flags. Pre-1.2.0 the --auth control is inert, so any --share launch stands up an unauthenticated training control plane; --share --auth is the false-safety case operators believed was protected. Rationale: Uses the exact CLI invocation surface from the advisory (backprop ui + --share/--auth). --share is the article's documented public-exposure flag and pre-1.2.0 makes the UI reachable with no working auth; matching --auth alongside surfaces the false-safety deployments the advisory calls out. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f65r-h4g3-3h9h • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/backpropagate/CVE-2026-48797/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-48797/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • ML engineer intentionally running 'backprop ui --share' behind a VPN/reverse proxy that adds its own auth
  • Post-upgrade (>=1.2.0) hosts where --auth now works but the command line still contains the flag
  • CI/CD or lab automation launching the UI with --share for smoke tests
  • Operator using --share only on a firewalled internal network
  • Shell history / documentation examples echoed into a terminal without actually binding a port
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ci-runner", "jenkins", "buildkite-agent")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host's installed backpropagate version (pip show backpropagate / package inventory) — if >=1.2.0 the auth is enforced and risk is low; if 1.1.0-1.1.1 with --share, treat as an exposed unauthenticated training plane. 2) Contain: kill the Reflex process, block inbound to the bound port (default 7860) at the host firewall, and if the UI was internet-reachable revoke/rotate the operator's HuggingFace token (Hub-push abuse vector). 3) Hunt: pull inbound connections to port 7860 from non-loopback sources, review rx.upload writes for attacker-dropped datasets, and check HF push history for unexpected repo targets.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "backprop" and ProcessCommandLine has "ui"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--share" or ProcessCommandLine has "--auth"
| extend PublicShare = ProcessCommandLine has "--share"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, PublicShare, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetProcessCommandLine has "backprop" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "backprop")
| where (TargetProcessCommandLine has "ui" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "ui")
| where (TargetProcessCommandLine has "--share" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "--auth" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "--share" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "--auth")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Host running vulnerable Backpropagate 1.1.0-1.1.1 (CVE-2026-48797) in software inventory AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces endpoints with the Backpropagate package in the affected 1.1.0-1.1.1 range where the Reflex UI auth guard is inert. This is a posture/attack-surface hunt to prioritise upgrades to 1.2.0 before an exposed UI is reached, keyed on the CVE and the concrete package/version range from the advisory. Rationale: Keys on the exact CVE id (CVE-2026-48797) and the advisory's affected version range (pip:backpropagate >=1.1.0,<1.2.0), so it enumerates the concrete attack surface without guessing behaviour. Vuln-inventory telemetry only, no endpoint noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-48797/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/backpropagate/CVE-2026-48797/ • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-48797-cwe-358-improperly-implemented-secu-63bfdfdd
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already scheduled/queued for the 1.2.0 upgrade in the current patch window
  • Isolated air-gapped GPU boxes where the UI is never launched with --share
  • Dev sandboxes intentionally kept on 1.1.x for reproducibility that never bind the UI
  • TVM version parsing quirks reporting 1.1.x npm @mcptoolshop/backpropagate separately from the pip package
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported version is truly 1.1.0 or 1.1.1 (not a mis-parsed 1.2.x) and whether the host has ever launched the Reflex UI. 2) Contain: schedule/push 'pip install --upgrade backpropagate' to >=1.2.0 (or @mcptoolshop/backpropagate@latest); if immediate upgrade is impossible, ensure the UI is only started with no flags (localhost bind) and reachable only via SSH port-forward. 3) Hunt: cross-reference these hosts against process-creation hits for 'backprop ui --share' and inbound connections to port 7860 to find any that were actually exposed.

Inbound access to exposed Backpropagate Reflex UI port 7860 from non-local source (CVE-2026-48797) AIExploitation Medium
Detects inbound network sessions to the Reflex training UI's default port 7860 originating from non-loopback/non-RFC1918 addresses. On an unpatched host launched with --share this is direct unauthenticated access to the training control plane (dataset read, training start, HuggingFace push), i.e. active exploitation rather than mere exposure. Rationale: Port 7860 is the Reflex/Gradio default the advisory itself references (ssh -L 7860:localhost:7860 workaround). Inbound from a public/non-RFC1918 source to that port on an unpatched host is the concrete exploitation shape for the unauthenticated UI, distinct from the process-launch and inventory pivots. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f65r-h4g3-3h9h • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-48797/
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote collaborator reaching a --share UI over a corporate egress IP that presents as public
  • Other apps that also default to port 7860 (Gradio demos, unrelated Reflex apps) on the same host
  • Vulnerability scanners / attack-surface tools probing 7860 across the estate
  • NAT/proxy hairpin making an internal client appear as a public source IP
  • Load-balancer or uptime-monitor health checks hitting the port
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python", "python3", "reflex", "backprop", "node")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the listening process on 7860 is the Backpropagate/Reflex UI (InitiatingProcessFileName python/reflex) and the host version is 1.1.0-1.1.1; identify the remote source IP and whether it is expected. 2) Contain: block inbound 7860 at host/perimeter firewall, terminate the Reflex process, and rotate the operator's HuggingFace token if the session was reachable. 3) Hunt: review rx.upload file writes and dataset-preview reads during the session window, enumerate any HuggingFace Hub push targets, and check for repeated/high-volume uploads indicating disk-fill DoS.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where LocalPort == 7860
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted", "ListeningConnectionCreated")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstPortNumber == 7860
| where NetworkDirection == "Inbound"
| where isnotempty(SrcIpAddr) and not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr)) and SrcIpAddr != "127.0.0.1"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, SrcIpAddr, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FortiBleed password-spray success burst against internet-facing Fortinet/edge auth AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a single source IP producing a high volume of failed authentications against a Fortinet appliance (SSL-VPN / admin login) followed by a successful login in the same window — the exact 'successful logins shortly after large-volume password failure events' pattern Unit 42 flags for the FortiBleed credential-spraying campaign. Rationale: Implements Unit 42's explicit FortiBleed guidance — audit remote-access logs for successful logins shortly after large-volume failure events — scoped to Fortinet auth via the CIM app values / DeviceVendor='Fortinet'. Threshold + same-window success join is what separates spray-then-compromise from routine VPN typos. Cross-checked with SOCRadar/SecurityWeek FortiBleed reporting and Arctic Wolf's CVE-2024-55591 analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/ • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1110.004 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote worker repeatedly fat-fingering an SSL-VPN password then succeeding
  • Misconfigured VPN client or saved-credential loop retrying stale creds before a successful re-auth
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanner (Qualys/Tenable) credential checks against the appliance
  • Shared NAT egress IP where many staff log in (inflated failure+success counts from one SourceIP)
  • Password-rotation day causing widespread first-attempt failures followed by success
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<populate watchlist: known scanner + corp NAT egress IPs via a Sentinel watchlist join, not inline>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the CompromisedUser + SourceIP; geolocate SourceIP and check whether the success used MFA and from a known ASN/country. Inspect the failed-user set — many distinct users from one IP = spray, not a typo. 2) Contain: if SourceIP is foreign/unrecognized, force-disable the compromised admin/VPN account, kill active SSL-VPN tunnels, block the SourceIP at the edge, and rotate the credential. 3) Hunt: from that SourceIP/account pivot to post-auth config changes (new admin accounts, sslvpn user groups), jsconsole admin logins, and any config download — feed into the FortiBleed jsconsole and rogue-admin UCs.
let lookback = 7d;
let window = 1h;
let Failed = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has "login" and (EventOutcome in~ ("failure","failed") or Message has_any ("login failed","Login failed","authentication failed","ssl-login-fail"))
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetUsers = dcount(DestinationHostName) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, window);
let Success = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has "login" and (EventOutcome in~ ("success","succeeded") or Message has_any ("login successful","SSL tunnel established"))
| summarize Successes = count(), CompromisedUser = make_set(DestinationHostName, 20) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, window);
Failed
| where Failures >= 30   // 30 = empirical spray burst floor per source per hour
| join kind=inner Success on SourceIP, TimeGenerated
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, Failures, TargetUsers, Successes, CompromisedUser
| order by Failures desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| stats sum(eval(if(action="failure",count,0))) as failures, sum(eval(if(action="success",count,0))) as successes, dc(user) as targeted_users, values(eval(if(action="success",user,null()))) as compromised_user, values(dest) as dest by src, _time
| where failures >= 30 and successes >= 1

| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`

| where failures >= 30 and successes >= 1

FortiGate jsconsole / loopback admin login (CVE-2024-55591 auth-bypass exploitation) AIExploitation High
Hunts the high-fidelity exploitation signature of CVE-2024-55591: administrative logins attributed to the 'jsconsole' interface and/or successful super-admin logins sourced from the device loopback/local IP — the artifact the Node.js websocket auth-bypass leaves when an unauthenticated attacker forges super_admin access on FortiOS/FortiProxy. Rationale: Uses the two corroborated CVE-2024-55591 exploitation artifacts — `ui=jsconsole` in the admin-login record (matched in CommonSecurityLog Message) and super-admin logins from the device loopback/local IP (CIM Authentication.src=127.0.0.1) — reported by Arctic Wolf, watchTowr ('I Am The Super_Admin Now') and Trustwave. Both are near-zero in benign FortiGate operation. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/ • https://labs.watchtowr.com/get-fortirekt-i-am-the-super_admin-now-fortios-authentication-bypass-cve-2024-55591/ • https://trustwave.com/en-us/resources/blogs/spiderlabs-blog/cve-2024-55591-fortinet-fortios-fortiproxy-zero-day

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Automation/orchestration tooling (Ansible/FortiManager) driving CLI via the local console
  • Internal penetration test replicating CVE-2024-55591
  • Health-check scripts hitting the management interface from a jump host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the jsconsole/loopback login corresponds to a real admin session — legitimate jsconsole use originates from an authenticated GUI session with a genuine admin SourceIP; exploitation shows loopback/local src and no preceding interactive auth. Check FortiOS version against the CVE-2024-55591 fixed builds. 2) Contain: isolate the device's management interface from the internet, disable/rotate all admin accounts, and capture the running + startup config for IR. 3) Hunt: enumerate admin accounts and sslvpn user groups created/modified after the first jsconsole login, look for `--userfrom`-style audit-record tampering, and any config download/exfil to chain with the rogue-admin and FortiBleed config-extraction UCs.

FortiGate rogue super_admin / SSL-VPN account creation following CVE-2024-55591 exploit AIInstallation High
Hunts post-exploitation persistence for the FortiBleed/CVE-2024-55591 chain: creation of new FortiGate administrator accounts (often random usernames) or new SSL-VPN local users / user groups via config changes. This is how attackers convert a one-shot auth bypass into durable, high-privilege access for offline-cracked credential re-use. Rationale: Targets the documented CVE-2024-55591 post-exploit actions — new admin accounts with random names, new SSL-VPN local users and groups — via Fortinet config-change logs (cfgpath system.admin / user.group) and the CIM Change datamodel (action=created, object_category=user). Account creation on an edge appliance is rare and tightly change-controlled, so FP is low. Corroborated by Arctic Wolf and Cyble. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/ • https://cyble.com/blog/cve-2024-55591-the-fortinet-flaw-putting-critical-systems-at-risk/

Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Planned admin onboarding by the network team during a change window
  • FortiManager/automation pushing a config template that provisions admin or VPN users
  • Legitimate SSL-VPN user-group expansion during an access-request rollout
  • MSP/managed-SOC provisioning a monitoring admin account
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the ActorAdmin and SourceIP that created the new object; correlate against an authorized change ticket and verify the actor session was not a jsconsole/loopback exploit login. Flag random-looking usernames. 2) Contain: delete or disable the unauthorized admin/VPN account and group, terminate its sessions, and rotate credentials for every legitimate admin on the device. 3) Hunt: review whether the new account granted VPN access, established tunnels into internal networks, or downloaded the device config; pivot on its SourceIP across other edge devices to scope the FortiBleed campaign footprint.

| where Message has_any ("super_admin","prof_admin","accprofile","sslvpn")
| where Message has_any ("Object attribute configured","Added","cfgattr","New","create")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, ActorAdmin = SourceUserName, NewObject = DestinationHostName, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FortiBleed MSSQL login-failure burst then success (internet-exposed SQL spraying) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the FortiBleed campaign's parallel targeting of internet-exposed MSSQL: a single client IP generating a burst of SQL Server login failures (error 18456) across one or many logins within a short window — the spray signature Unit 42 observed against MSSQL devices alongside Fortinet and Sophos. Rationale: Covers the article's explicit observation that the FortiBleed actors also targeted MSSQL devices. Pivots on SQL Server error 18456 (login failed) parsed for CLIENT IP and login name in Sentinel's Event table, with a Defender DeviceLogonEvents fallback for Windows-auth brute force against the SQL host and a CIM Authentication path for Splunk. Threshold-based, so framed as a burst detector. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Application/service account with a stale connection string hammering the DB after a password change

Response runbook

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")

TinyRCT backdoor masquerading as PerfWatson2.exe executing from %LOCALAPPDATA% AIInstallation High
Hunts the CL-STA-1062 TinyRCT .NET backdoor, which masquerades as Visual Studio's PerfWatson2.exe but enforces an environment check that it runs only from %LOCALAPPDATA%. Legitimate PerfWatson2.exe ships inside the Visual Studio install tree under Program Files, so any PerfWatson2.exe launching from AppData\Local is article-specific TinyRCT behaviour. Rationale: Uses the article's exact masquerade name PerfWatson2.exe plus TinyRCT's own self-imposed %LOCALAPPDATA% execution constraint; legitimate PerfWatson2 lives under Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio, making AppData\Local execution near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/taiwan-web-servers-breached-by-uat-7237.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1497.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer running a portable/extracted copy of Visual Studio components from a profile folder
  • Visual Studio installer caching PerfWatson2 in AppData during an update (rare, usually Program Files)
  • Security tooling copying the binary to AppData for analysis on an analyst workstation
  • EDR sandbox detonation copying the sample into LocalAppData
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\" and not(FolderPath has @"\Microsoft Visual Studio\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and confirm it is not the signed Microsoft PerfWatson2 (legit is signed 'Microsoft Corporation' under Program Files). Check the parent process and whether the host concurrently beaconed to 45.32.113.172 or 139.180.134.221. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and quarantine the AppData\Local copy; block both C2 IPs at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: search the environment for any PerfWatson2.exe outside Program Files, for the GoogleUpdater scheduled task, and for choice.exe-based self-delete batch chains indicating TinyRCT cleanup.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "PerfWatson2.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\PerfWatson2.exe"
| where NewProcessName has @"\AppData\Local\"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound connection to CL-STA-1062 / TinyRCT C2 and tool-staging infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host connecting to the two confirmed CL-STA-1062 IPs: 45.32.113.172 (TinyRCT HTTP C2, ~10s beacon) and 139.180.134.221 (payload/tool-staging server hosting the PerfWatson2.exe backdoor and RAR tool archives). Pure-IOC network detection for both beaconing and payload pull. Rationale: Both IPs are explicitly named in the article (139.180.134.221 hosting PerfWatson2.exe; 45.32.113.172 as TinyRCT C2 in the kill-chain block) and confirmed across the Unit 42 report and Talos UAT-7237 overlap; raw IOC hits are high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher or sandbox sandboxing the sample and reaching the C2
  • Threat-intel scanning/validation services probing the IPs from a corporate range
  • Shared Vultr/cloud hosting reassigning the IP to a benign tenant after takedown (verify timestamps against report publication)
  • Internal vuln scanner configured to crawl flagged IOCs
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process; if it is PerfWatson2.exe, a fake vmtools.exe, or curl.exe from a web-server context, treat as confirmed. Note beacon cadence (~10s = TinyRCT). 2) Contain: block both IPs at firewall/proxy, isolate the source host, and capture memory before reboot. 3) Hunt: pivot on src_ip for prior 139.180.134.221 downloads (RAR/SoftEther tool pulls), and sweep all hosts for second-stage payloads delivered from the staging server.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.32.113.172", "139.180.134.221")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("45.32.113.172", "139.180.134.221")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SoftEther VPN / VNT tunneler masquerading as VMware vmtools.exe AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts CL-STA-1062's habit of disguising tunneling tools (SoftEther VPN, VNT) as VMware system binaries such as vmtools.exe. Flags processes named vmtools/vmtoolsd whose signing company is not 'VMware, Inc.' or whose product string references SoftEther — i.e. a VMware-named binary that isn't VMware. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's Figure 6/7 masquerade (SoftEther disguised as vmtools.exe, VNT disguised as a VMware executable); the company-name/path mismatch separates the tunneler from genuine VMware Tools without needing a hash. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/taiwan-web-servers-breached-by-uat-7237.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine VMware Tools where version metadata is stripped/empty after repackaging by an MSP
  • Older VMware Tools builds signed under a legacy company string ('VMware, Inc.' variations)
  • Third-party VM management tools legitimately named vmtools running from a non-standard path
  • Software-distribution systems staging VMware Tools in a temp folder before install
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\VMware\VMware Tools\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the binary's digital signature and the command line for SoftEther/VNT tunnel arguments (server address, listen port). Confirm it isn't VMware-signed. 2) Contain: terminate the tunneler, isolate the host, and block its configured remote VPN/relay endpoint. 3) Hunt: look for scheduled tasks launching the same disguised binary, RDP sessions riding the tunnel, and the same masquerade name on peer hosts indicating lateral spread.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("vmtools.exe", "vmtoolsd.exe")
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "VMware, Inc." or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "SoftEther"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("vmtools.exe", "vmtoolsd.exe")
| where ActingProcessFileCompany != "VMware, Inc." or ActingProcessFileProduct has "SoftEther"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessFileCompany, ActingProcessFileProduct, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("vmtools.exe","vmtoolsd.exe") AND NOT Processes.process_path="*\\VMware\\*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("vmtools.exe","vmtoolsd.exe") AND NOT Processes.process_path="*\\VMware\\*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Scheduled task persistence for GoogleUpdater or VMware-disguised VNT binary AIInstallation Medium
Detects CL-STA-1062 establishing persistence via schtasks.exe creating a task named GoogleUpdater (TinyRCT loader) or a task launching a tunneler disguised as vmtools/VNT (Figure 7). Pivots on the task-creation command line rather than the binary itself. Rationale: Combines the article/kill-chain GoogleUpdater task name (TinyRCT loader) with the Figure 7 VNT-as-VMware scheduled task; task creation referencing these masquerade tokens is far more specific than generic schtasks alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Google Chrome/Updater creating GoogleUpdateTaskMachineCore tasks (note: name differs from 'GoogleUpdater')
  • VMware Tools installer registering a legitimate vmtools-related task
  • Admin scripts re-creating VMware service tasks during template provisioning
  • Software-packaging tools that template task names containing 'vmtools'
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "GoogleUpdateTaskMachine" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\VMware\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full task action (the binary path and arguments the task launches) and verify whether it points to a signed Google/VMware binary in its standard location. 2) Contain: delete the malicious task, isolate the host, and quarantine the referenced binary. 3) Hunt: enumerate all scheduled tasks across the fleet for the same name/binary, and correlate the task creator process — if it was a web shell (w3wp.exe) or PerfWatson2.exe, escalate to full IR.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("GoogleUpdater", "vmtools", "VNT")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any ("GoogleUpdater", "vmtools", "VNT")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Scheduled Task Creation for GoogleUpdater or VMware-Disguised Tunneler

IIS web shell (w3wp.exe) spawning recon, curl exfil, or RAR staging AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CL-STA-1062 ASPX web-shell command-execution channel where the IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawns cmd/curl/rar and native recon binaries — the actor piped system/network enumeration to actor IPs via curl and staged source code into RAR archives directly from the web shell. Rationale: Encodes the article's web-shell-as-execution-mechanism (Figure 4 curl enumeration, Figure 2 source-code archiving) via the w3wp.exe parent pivot — IIS workers should virtually never spawn curl, rar, tracert, or whoami. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/08/taiwan-web-servers-breached-by-uat-7237.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web applications shelling out to net.exe/whoami for diagnostics
  • Application deployment scripts invoking cmd.exe under the app pool identity
  • Monitoring agents that run ipconfig/netstat from a web context
  • Developer health-check endpoints that exec systeminfo
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck", "\\Monitoring\\") and FileName in~ ("ipconfig.exe","netstat.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child command lines — recon piped to curl targeting 45.32.113.172/139.180.134.221 or rar with -hp confirms malicious use; review IIS logs for the requesting URI and source IP (the web shell). 2) Contain: pull the offending .aspx file, isolate the web server, and reset the app-pool service account credentials. 3) Hunt: enumerate recently written/modified .aspx files in web roots, and pivot on the source IP across other internet-facing servers for the same web-shell pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe", "httpd.exe", "php-cgi.exe", "tomcat.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "curl.exe", "rar.exe", "whoami.exe", "ipconfig.exe", "net.exe", "net1.exe", "tracert.exe", "systeminfo.exe", "netstat.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe", @"\curl.exe", @"\rar.exe", @"\whoami.exe", @"\ipconfig.exe", @"\net.exe", @"\net1.exe", @"\tracert.exe", @"\systeminfo.exe", @"\netstat.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: IIS Worker w3wp.exe Spawning Recon, Curl, or RAR (Web Shell Command Execution)
id: e15b7d33-9c2a-4f7e-8b04-6d3a1e9c5f72
description: Detects the IIS worker process spawning command shell, curl, RAR, or native recon utilities, consistent with CL-STA-1062 ASPX web-shell command execution and curl-based enumeration exfil.

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@ParentImage:*\w3wp.exe OR @ParentImage:*\W3WP.exe) (@Image:*\cmd.exe OR @Image:*\curl.exe OR @Image:*\rar.exe OR @Image:*\whoami.exe OR @Image:*\ipconfig.exe OR @Image:*\net.exe OR @Image:*\tracert.exe OR @Image:*\systeminfo.exe OR @Image:*\netstat.exe)

Password-protected RAR staging of data for exfiltration (-hp) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts CL-STA-1062's data-staging step: compressing findings (MSSQL dumps, entire web-server source-code directories) into header-encrypted, password-protected RAR archives using the rar -hp flag prior to exfil. Pivots on the -hp<password> add-to-archive command line, which survives binary renaming. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit tradecraft of compressing findings into password-protected RAR archives; the -hp<password> token (header encryption with an inline password) is rarely used by legitimate users and is the actor's recurring staging signature. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7237-targets-web-hosting-infra/
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admins archiving log bundles or backups with a password for transport
  • Legitimate use of WinRAR with -hp by a power user securing personal data
  • Backup software that wraps RAR with header encryption
  • Developers packaging release artifacts with a protected archive
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe", "backup.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Backup\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the archive path and contents source — large archives built from web roots, database export folders, or user document trees signal staging. Check which process invoked rar (web shell = high severity). 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve the archive, and watch for immediate outbound transfer to the actor IPs. 3) Hunt: correlate the archive creation time with subsequent curl/POST egress and SoftEther tunnel activity; sweep peer hosts for the same -hp pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-hp\S+"
| where ProcessCommandLine has " a "
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s-hp\S+"
| where CommandLine has " a "
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
